claim: Plant-herbivore interactions dominate the planet's terrestrial ecology.
source: Plant-herbivore interactions dominate the planet's terrestrial ecology.
evidence: This is a general statement about ecological relationships presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Insects are among the most versatile evolutionary innovators when it comes to host-plant specialization.
source: When it comes to host–plant specialization, insects are among the most versatile evolutionary innovators, able to disarm multiple chemical plant defenses.
evidence: This is a general statement about insect evolution presented without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Insects are able to disarm multiple chemical plant defenses.
source: When it comes to host–plant specialization, insects are among the most versatile evolutionary innovators, able to disarm multiple chemical plant defenses.
evidence: This is a general statement about insect capabilities presented as established knowledge.

claim: Sequestration is a widespread strategy to detoxify noxious metabolites.
source: Sequestration is a widespread strategy to detoxify noxious metabolites, frequently for the insect's own benefit against predation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about insect defense strategies.

claim: Sequestration is frequently used for the insect's own benefit against predation.
source: Sequestration is a widespread strategy to detoxify noxious metabolites, frequently for the insect's own benefit against predation.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the function of sequestration.

claim: CpMRP is an ATP-binding cassette transporter of the poplar leaf beetle, Chrysomela populi.
source: In this study, we describe the broad-spectrum ATP-binding cassette transporter CpMRP of the poplar leaf beetle, Chrysomela populi as the first candidate involved in the sequestration of phytochemicals in insects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by sequence analysis and functional characterization.

claim: CpMRP is a broad-spectrum transporter.
source: In this study, we describe the broad-spectrum ATP-binding cassette transporter CpMRP of the poplar leaf beetle, Chrysomela populi as the first candidate involved in the sequestration of phytochemicals in insects.
evidence: This is supported by comparative transport assays showing CpMRP transports multiple glucoside substrates.

claim: CpMRP is the first candidate involved in the sequestration of phytochemicals in insects.
source: In this study, we describe the broad-spectrum ATP-binding cassette transporter CpMRP of the poplar leaf beetle, Chrysomela populi as the first candidate involved in the sequestration of phytochemicals in insects.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the study based on the novel identification and functional characterization of CpMRP.

claim: CpMRP acts in the defensive glands of the larvae.
source: CpMRP acts in the defensive glands of the larvae as a pacemaker for the irreversible shuttling of pre-selected metabolites from the hemolymph into defensive secretions.
evidence: This is supported by transcript abundance data and immunohistochemical localization showing CpMRP is highly expressed in defensive glands.

claim: CpMRP functions as a pacemaker for the irreversible shuttling of pre-selected metabolites from the hemolymph into defensive secretions.
source: CpMRP acts in the defensive glands of the larvae as a pacemaker for the irreversible shuttling of pre-selected metabolites from the hemolymph into defensive secretions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on transport assays, localization data, and RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Silencing CpMRP in vivo creates a defenseless phenotype.
source: Silencing CpMRP in vivo creates a defenseless phenotype, indicating its role in the secretion process is crucial.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing larvae lack defensive secretions after CpMRP knockdown.

claim: CpMRP's role in the secretion process is crucial.
source: Silencing CpMRP in vivo creates a defenseless phenotype, indicating its role in the secretion process is crucial.
evidence: This is inferred from the defenseless phenotype observed upon CpMRP knockdown.

claim: Sequences similar to CpMRP were identified in the defensive glands of related leaf beetle species.
source: In the defensive glands of related leaf beetle species, we identified sequences similar to CpMRP and assume therefore that exocrine gland-based defensive strategies, evolved by these insects to repel their enemies, rely on ABC transporters as a key element.
evidence: This is supported by sequence identification in P. cochleariae and C. lapponica showing high amino acid identity to CpMRP.

claim: Exocrine gland-based defensive strategies in leaf beetles rely on ABC transporters as a key element.
source: In the defensive glands of related leaf beetle species, we identified sequences similar to CpMRP and assume therefore that exocrine gland-based defensive strategies, evolved by these insects to repel their enemies, rely on ABC transporters as a key element.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of CpMRP homologs in related species with similar defensive systems.

claim: Insects have relied on plants as a food source for millions of years.
source: For millions of years, insects have relied on plants as a food source.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about insect-plant evolutionary history.

claim: Plants have developed toxic secondary metabolite production to impede herbivory.
source: To impede herbivory, plants have developed several morphological and biochemical traits; one of those is based on toxic secondary metabolite production.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about plant defense mechanisms.

claim: Insects have evolved detoxification strategies including sequestration to overcome chemical plant defenses.
source: Insects, in turn, have evolved ingenious detoxification strategies, including the process of sequestration, to overcome the chemical plant defenses (Sorensen and Dearing, 2006; Li et al., 2007; Opitz and Muller, 2009; Boeckler et al., 2011; Winde and Wittstock, 2011; Dobler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on insect detoxification strategies.

claim: Insect counter-mechanisms affect the ecology and evolution of plants.
source: These counter-mechanisms thereby affect the ecology and evolution of plants (Ehrlich and Raven, 1964; Agrawal et al., 2012; Hare, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on plant-insect coevolution.

claim: Sequestration involves the uptake, transfer, and concentration of occasionally modified phytochemicals into the hemolymph, cuticle, specialized tissues or glands.
source: The phenomenon of sequestration involves the uptake, transfer, and concentration of occasionally modified phytochemicals into the hemolymph, cuticle, specialized tissues or glands.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the sequestration process.

claim: Numerous species from almost all insect orders have evolved the ability to sequester chemicals.
source: Numerous species from almost all insect orders have evolved the ability to sequester chemicals (Duffey, 1980; Nishida, 2002; Opitz and Muller, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on chemical sequestration in insects.

claim: Sequestered toxins are frequently used by insects for their own defense, as is the case in leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae).
source: Frequently the sequestered toxins are used by insects for their own defense, as is the case in leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) (Meinwald et al., 1977; Pasteels et al., 1990; Gillespie et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on leaf beetle defenses.

claim: The most comprehensive knowledge of sequestration processes has been obtained from juveniles of leaf beetles belonging to the taxon Chrysomelina.
source: Up to now, the most comprehensive knowledge of sequestration processes has been obtained from juveniles of the leaf beetles belonging to the taxon Chrysomelina (Soetens et al., 1998; Termonia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on Chrysomelina sequestration.

claim: The chemical defenses of Chrysomelina larvae are made up of compounds that are either sequestered from their host plants or synthesized de novo.
source: The chemical defenses of these larvae are made up of compounds that are either sequestered from their host plants or synthesized de novo.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about Chrysomelina larval defenses.

claim: Defensive compounds in Chrysomelina larvae are transferred into nine pairs of specialized exocrine glands found on the back of the larvae.
source: Regardless of their origin, these compounds are transferred into nine pairs of specialized exocrine glands that are found on the back of the larvae (Hinton, 1951; Pasteels and Rowell-Rahier, 1991; Pasteels, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous morphological studies of Chrysomelina larvae.

claim: Each defensive gland is composed of a number of enlarged secretory cells connected to a chitin-coated reservoir.
source: According to morphological studies, each defensive gland is composed of a number of enlarged secretory cells, which are in turn connected to a chitin-coated reservoir.
evidence: This is based on previous morphological studies of gland structure.

claim: Secretory cells are always accompanied by two canal cells that form a cuticular canal connecting the secretory cell with the reservoir.
source: The secretory cells are always accompanied by two canal cells that form a cuticular canal, which connects the secretory cell with the reservoir (Noirot and Quennedy, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous morphological studies.

claim: When disturbed, juvenile beetles evert their glandular reservoirs and present droplets of secretions.
source: When disturbed, the juvenile beetles evert their glandular reservoirs and present droplets of secretions.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about larval defensive behavior.

claim: In Chrysomelina larvae, all compounds reaching the glandular reservoir via the hemolymph are glucosides.
source: In Chrysomelina larvae, all compounds reaching the glandular reservoir via the hemolymph are glucosides that are converted enzymatically into the biologically active form within the reservoir (Pasteels et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on Chrysomelina defensive chemistry.

claim: Glucosides are converted enzymatically into the biologically active form within the reservoir.
source: In Chrysomelina larvae, all compounds reaching the glandular reservoir via the hemolymph are glucosides that are converted enzymatically into the biologically active form within the reservoir (Pasteels et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on enzymatic conversion in the reservoir.

claim: The glands secrete enzymes for the final metabolic conversion of precursors into defensive compounds in the reservoir.
source: Thus, the glands also secrete enzymes for the final metabolic conversion of precursors into defensive compounds in the reservoir.
evidence: This is inferred from the enzymatic conversion of glucosides in the reservoir.

claim: The ability to sequester plant glucosides is considered an energy-saving, monotypic adaptation within Chrysomelina.
source: The ability to sequester plant glucosides is considered an energy-saving, monotypic adaptation within Chrysomelina (Figure 1B), given the phylogenetic evidence that this process evolved from an ancestral autogenous biosynthesis of deterrent monoterpenes (iridoids) (Termonia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic evidence cited from previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Sequestration of plant glucosides evolved from an ancestral autogenous biosynthesis of deterrent monoterpenes (iridoids).
source: The ability to sequester plant glucosides is considered an energy-saving, monotypic adaptation within Chrysomelina (Figure 1B), given the phylogenetic evidence that this process evolved from an ancestral autogenous biosynthesis of deterrent monoterpenes (iridoids) (Termonia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Chrysomela populi is an obligate-sequestering species.
source: The poplar leaf beetle Chrysomela populi, is an example of an obligate-sequestering species, and its larvae incorporate the phenolglucoside salicin from the leaves of their salicaceaous food plants (Pasteels et al., 1983; Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on C. populi feeding behavior.

claim: Chrysomela populi larvae incorporate the phenolglucoside salicin from the leaves of their salicaceous food plants.
source: The poplar leaf beetle Chrysomela populi, is an example of an obligate-sequestering species, and its larvae incorporate the phenolglucoside salicin from the leaves of their salicaceaous food plants (Pasteels et al., 1983; Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on C. populi sequestration.

claim: In the reservoir of C. populi defensive glands, salicin is metabolized into the volatile deterrent salicylaldehyde.
source: In the reservoir of their defensive glands, the salicin is then metabolized into the volatile deterrent salicylaldehyde (Michalski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on salicin metabolism.

claim: In Chrysomela lapponica, several glucosidically bound alcohols are simultaneously imported, resulting in a diversity of compounds, especially esters, in the larval exudate.
source: Additionally, in Chrysomela lapponica several glucosidically bound alcohols are simultaneously imported, resulting in a diversity of compounds, especially of esters, in the exudate of the larvae (Hilker and Schulz, 1994; Schulz et al., 1997; Kirsch et al., 2011; Tolzin-Banasch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on C. lapponica defensive chemistry.

claim: Physiological studies using thioglucosides have indicated a complex influx-efflux transport network that guides plant-derived glucosides through the insect body.
source: Physiological studies on de novo iridoid-producing, salicin sequestering, and ester-producing larvae using thioglucosides have indicated a complex influx–efflux transport network that guides the plant-derived glucosides through the insect body (Discher et al., 2009; Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous physiological studies.

claim: Presumed intestinal carriers in the gut epithelial cells allow a broad spectrum of secondary metabolites to enter the hemolymph.
source: Presumed intestinal carriers in the gut epithelial cells allow a broad spectrum of secondary metabolites to enter the hemolymph, a process that is accompanied by a similar non-selective excretion via the Malpighian tubules.
evidence: This is based on inference from physiological studies and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: Non-selective excretion of secondary metabolites occurs via the Malpighian tubules.
source: Presumed intestinal carriers in the gut epithelial cells allow a broad spectrum of secondary metabolites to enter the hemolymph, a process that is accompanied by a similar non-selective excretion via the Malpighian tubules.
evidence: This is based on inference from physiological studies.

claim: Thioglucosides are selectively accumulated up to 500-fold into the reservoir from a hemolymph pool.
source: Furthermore, thioglucosides are being selectively accumulated, up to 500-fold, into the reservoir from a hemolymph pool, suggesting an active transport system is at work (Feld et al., 2001; Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies measuring thioglucoside accumulation.

claim: The selective accumulation of thioglucosides suggests an active transport system is at work.
source: Furthermore, thioglucosides are being selectively accumulated, up to 500-fold, into the reservoir from a hemolymph pool, suggesting an active transport system is at work (Feld et al., 2001; Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the high accumulation factor observed in previous studies.

claim: Active ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters are well-known key-components of various detoxification mechanisms in all phyla of life.
source: The active ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters are well-known key-components of various detoxification mechanisms in all phyla of life (Sipos and Kuchler, 2006; Leprohon et al., 2011; Holland, 2011; Broehan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on ABC transporters.

claim: In eukaryotes, ABC transporters translocate a wide variety of compounds from the cytoplasm to the extracellular space or to intracellular compartments.
source: In eukaryotes, they translocate a wide variety of compounds from the cytoplasm to the extracellular space or to intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about ABC transporter function.

claim: The role of ABC transporters in the sequestration of plant secondary metabolites in insect herbivores has not yet been investigated.
source: Their role in the sequestration of plant secondary metabolites in insect herbivores, however, has not yet been investigated (Karnaky et al., 2000; Sorensen and Dearing, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating a gap in previous research.

claim: CpMRP displays an exceptionally high transcript level in the glandular tissue, exceeding that in the gut and Malpighian tubules by more than 7000-fold.
source: Screening of expression levels of transcript sequences encoding ABC transporter motifs revealed a putative candidate, referred to here as CpMRP. It displayed an exceptionally high transcript level in the glandular tissue, exceeding that in the gut and Malpighian tubules by more than 7000-fold (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The deduced amino acid sequence of cpmrp contains 1331 residues (154.9 kDa).
source: Among all known and functionally characterized ABC transporters, the deduced amino acid sequence of cpmrp, which contained 1331 residues (154.9 kDa), shares the highest sequence similarity of 61% (41% sequence identity) to the human homologous multidrug resistance-associated protein MRP4 (ABC subfamily C) (Lee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the cloned cpmrp gene.

claim: CpMRP shares the highest sequence similarity of 61% (41% sequence identity) to the human multidrug resistance-associated protein MRP4 (ABC subfamily C).
source: Among all known and functionally characterized ABC transporters, the deduced amino acid sequence of cpmrp, which contained 1331 residues (154.9 kDa), shares the highest sequence similarity of 61% (41% sequence identity) to the human homologous multidrug resistance-associated protein MRP4 (ABC subfamily C) (Lee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and comparison with known ABC transporters, supported by citation.

claim: The predicted protein of CpMRP possesses the typical structural elements of ABC transporters.
source: The predicted protein of CpMRP from C. populi possesses the typical structural elements of ABC transporters (Zolnerciks et al., 2011); these consist of four domains: two TMDs (transmembrane domains), harboring six proposed transmembrane spans and two NBDs (nucleotide-binding domains), containing Walker A and B boxes (sequences GPVGAGKS and VYLMD, respectively), separated by an ABC signature motif (sequence LSGGQRARINLARAI).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with known ABC transporter structures, supported by citation.

claim: CpMRP consists of four domains: two TMDs harboring six proposed transmembrane spans and two NBDs containing Walker A and B boxes separated by an ABC signature motif.
source: The predicted protein of CpMRP from C. populi possesses the typical structural elements of ABC transporters (Zolnerciks et al., 2011); these consist of four domains: two TMDs (transmembrane domains), harboring six proposed transmembrane spans and two NBDs (nucleotide-binding domains), containing Walker A and B boxes (sequences GPVGAGKS and VYLMD, respectively), separated by an ABC signature motif (sequence LSGGQRARINLARAI).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis identifying characteristic ABC transporter motifs.

claim: 3D structure modeling of CpMRP supports the conclusions of the sequence alignment and illustrates the localization of characteristic sequence motifs.
source: Additionally, we conducted a 3D structure modeling of CpMRP (Figure 2D) to support the conclusions of the sequence alignment and to illustrate the localization of characteristic sequence motifs.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sequence alignment and structure modeling suggest that CpMRP is very likely an ABC transporter.
source: Both sequence alignment and structure modeling suggest that the newly identified protein CpMRP is very likely an ABC transporter.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis and structural modeling data.

claim: In Phaedon cochleariae, a sequence with 86% amino acid identity to CpMRP was identified.
source: In the ancestral de novo iridoid-producing species Phaedon cochleariae, we have identified a sequence with 86% amino acid identity to CpMRP and in the more derived species C. lapponica we identified a homolog of CpMRP sharing 93.7% amino acid identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of homologous genes in related species.

claim: In C. lapponica, a homolog of CpMRP sharing 93.7% amino acid identity was identified.
source: In the ancestral de novo iridoid-producing species Phaedon cochleariae, we have identified a sequence with 86% amino acid identity to CpMRP and in the more derived species C. lapponica we identified a homolog of CpMRP sharing 93.7% amino acid identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of homologous genes in related species.

claim: CpMRP homologs in P. cochleariae and C. lapponica share the same transcription pattern as CpMRP, being highly expressed in the larval glands only.
source: Both the sequences share the same transcription pattern like CpMRP, being highly expressed in the larval glands only (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is a highly conserved ABC transporter among Chrysomelina species that has an important ecological role.
source: Altogether this suggests that there is a highly conserved ABC transporter among Chrysomelina species that has an important ecological role.
evidence: This is inferred from the high sequence conservation and similar expression patterns of CpMRP homologs.

claim: The defensive system in Chrysomelina larvae has uniform architecture and morphology.
source: Given the uniform architecture and morphology of the defensive system (Hinton, 1951; Noirot and Quennedy, 1974) in Chrysomelina larvae, we expect functional similarities on the molecular level.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous morphological studies.

claim: Functional similarities on the molecular level are expected among Chrysomelina larvae.
source: Given the uniform architecture and morphology of the defensive system (Hinton, 1951; Noirot and Quennedy, 1974) in Chrysomelina larvae, we expect functional similarities on the molecular level.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological conservation and the identification of conserved CpMRP homologs.

claim: CpMRP was exclusively localized in the defensive glands.
source: The staining of full-body sections from juvenile C. populi showed that CpMRP was exclusively localized in the defensive glands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CpMRP was not present in the canal-forming cells or in the canal itself.
source: In more detail, CpMRP was present neither in the canal-forming cells (Figure 3A—C1, C2) nor in the canal itself (Figure 3Bb—Cc) but, rather in the secretory cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: CpMRP is present in the secretory cells.
source: In more detail, CpMRP was present neither in the canal-forming cells (Figure 3A—C1, C2) nor in the canal itself (Figure 3Bb—Cc) but, rather in the secretory cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: The intracellular distribution of CpMRP resembles a hollow sphere with a distinct reticular pattern.
source: Intriguingly, mapping CpMRP at subcellular magnification provided evidence for the exclusive localization within the secretory cells attached to the reservoir. The intracellular distribution of CpMRP resembles a hollow sphere with a distinct reticular pattern (arrows in Figure 3C, Figure 3E, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution immunohistochemical imaging shown in Figure 3 and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: CpMRP's intracellular presence in vesicular and reticular structures was corroborated by its co-localization with Bodipy-stained intracellular membranes.
source: Its intracellular presence in vesicular and reticular structures (Figure 3Bc) was corroborated by its co-localization with Bodipy-stained intracellular membranes (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: CpMRP was not detected in the basal lamina or in the adjacent basal infoldings.
source: Starting at the outside of the secretory cell, CpMRP was not detected in the basal lamina or in the adjacent basal infoldings (∼5 µm) (indicated with Bi in Figure 3Ba,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3.

claim: Directly after the basal infoldings, there is a sharp transition to a spherical zone of about 2-5 µm where the most dense CpMRP presence within the entire cell is observed.
source: Instead, directly after the basal infoldings, we observed a sharp transition to a spherical zone of about 2–5 µm; here, we noted the most dense CpMRP presence within the entire cell (Figure 3A–C [inset arrow] and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figures 2D and 3.

claim: The subcellular localization of CpMRP correlates with cellular storage compartments as demonstrated by vacuolar esterase activity.
source: Moreover, according to vacuolar esterase activity, demonstrated by CDCFDA staining (Pringle et al., 1989), the subcellular localization of CpMRP (Figure 3F,G [inset arrow]) correlates with cellular storage compartments (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by CDCFDA staining shown in Figure 3F,G and comparison with CpMRP localization.

claim: Silencing cpmrp had no influence on larval growth.
source: By comparing developmental traits among C. populi larvae after injecting cpmrp-dsRNA or gfp-dsRNA as a control, we found that silencing cpmrp had no influence on larval growth (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by body mass measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: About 10 days post-injection, the cpmrp knockdown larvae completely lost their ability to respond to stimulation with droplets of defensive secretion.
source: However, about 10 days post-injection, the cpmrp knockdown larvae completely lost their ability to respond to stimulation with droplets of defensive secretion (Figures 4B and 2B).
evidence: This is supported by secretion measurements shown in Figures 4B and 2B.

claim: The secretions began to diminish at day 8 post-injection.
source: The secretions began to diminish at day 8.
evidence: This is based on observations of secretion levels over time in RNAi experiments.

claim: cpmrp mRNA was reduced to a basal level of 15-20% within 2-3 days and persisted until the larvae pupated.
source: On the basis of transcript abundance, cpmrp mRNA was reduced to a basal level of 15–20% within 2–3 days and persisted until the larvae pupated (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At day 3 post-injection, both the cpmrp knocked-down and control secretory cells displayed a similar pattern of CpMRP distribution.
source: At day 3 post-injection, both the cpmrp knocked-down and control secretory cells displayed a similar pattern of CpMRP distribution (Figure 4Da,b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At later time points, the CpMRP expression in the RNAi group was strongly reduced in comparison to the gfp control.
source: At later time points, however, the CpMRP expression in the RNAi group was strongly reduced in comparison to the gfp control (Figure 4Dc—f), which is in agreement with Western blot analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 4D and Western blot in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CpMRP decayed exponentially to a relatively low basal level with a half-life of about 1 day.
source: CpMRP decayed exponentially to a relatively low basal level with a half-life of about 1 day, suggesting a degradation of CpMRP that is linearly proportional to its concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of CpMRP degradation kinetics shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The degradation of CpMRP is linearly proportional to its concentration.
source: CpMRP decayed exponentially to a relatively low basal level with a half-life of about 1 day, suggesting a degradation of CpMRP that is linearly proportional to its concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential decay kinetics observed in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Proportional protein degradation has been reported in human hepatocytes.
source: This proportionality has already been reported in human hepatocytes (Pereg et al., 2010; Popov et al., 2010; Nakagawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on protein degradation.

claim: The half-life of ABC transporters MDR1 and MDR2 in hepatocytes is 5 days.
source: Compared to a half-life of 5 days for the ABC transporters MDR1 and MDR2 reported in hepatocytes (Kipp and Arias, 2002), the rate of CpMRP turnover seems relatively high.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on ABC transporter turnover.

claim: The rate of CpMRP turnover seems relatively high compared to MDR1 and MDR2.
source: Compared to a half-life of 5 days for the ABC transporters MDR1 and MDR2 reported in hepatocytes (Kipp and Arias, 2002), the rate of CpMRP turnover seems relatively high.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of CpMRP half-life (1 day) with MDR1/MDR2 half-life (5 days).

claim: Secretory cells tended to increase the size of storage compartments, presumably vacuoles, in CpMRP knockdown larvae.
source: Qualitative microscopic observations showed that secretory cells tended to increase the size of storage compartments, presumably vacuoles, of the CpMRP knockdown larvae.
evidence: This is based on qualitative microscopic observations of knockdown larvae.

claim: CpMRP is a transporter for salicin.
source: Our transport studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes revealed that CpMRP is a transporter for salicin (Figure 5A), the naturally sequestered host–plant precursor of C. populi.
evidence: This is supported by transport assays in Xenopus oocytes shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Salicin is the naturally sequestered host-plant precursor of C. populi.
source: Our transport studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes revealed that CpMRP is a transporter for salicin (Figure 5A), the naturally sequestered host–plant precursor of C. populi.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about C. populi sequestration.

claim: CpMRP did not discriminate significantly between salicin, 8-hydroxygeraniol-O-glucoside, and phenylethyl-S-glucoside.
source: However, CpMRP did not discriminate significantly between the substrates.
evidence: This is supported by comparative transport assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For phenylethyl-S-glucoside and thiosalicin, the transport activity of CpMRP was slightly reduced compared to salicin.
source: For phenylethyl-S-glucoside and thiosalicin (6) the transport activity of CpMRP was slightly reduced compared to salicin (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative transport assays shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The sugar moiety of the substrates significantly lowered the transport activity of CpMRP.
source: Moreover, the sugar moiety of the substrates (comparing salicin and its galactoside analogue (4) (Figure 5D), further significantly lowered the transport activity of CpMRP, which is consistent with previous data obtained by feeding experiments (Kuhn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by comparative transport assays shown in Figure 5D and is consistent with previous feeding experiments.

claim: CpMRP has an apparent Km of 5.8 mM for salicin.
source: Based on the apparent Km of 5.8 (mM) for salicin, CpMRP (Figure 5B) seems to be a low-affinity transporter.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of salicin transport shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CpMRP seems to be a low-affinity transporter.
source: Based on the apparent Km of 5.8 (mM) for salicin, CpMRP (Figure 5B) seems to be a low-affinity transporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the relatively high Km value measured for salicin.

claim: CpMRP functions as a low-affinity glucoside transporter with a broad glucoside spectrum.
source: From our comparative transport assays we assume that CpMRP functions as low-affinity glucoside transporter with a broad glucoside spectrum.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data and comparative transport assays showing broad substrate specificity.

claim: Within the zone of highest CpMRP density, salicin is trapped in storage vesicles as soon as it enters the secretory cells.
source: We assume that within the described zone of highest CpMRP density (Figure 3A,B,D), salicin is trapped in storage vesicles as soon as it enters the secretory cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on CpMRP localization and transport activity data.

claim: The constant vesicular accumulation of plant glucoside precursors and further irreversible translocation into the reservoir keeps the glucoside concentration low inside the secretory cell.
source: The constant vesicular accumulation of plant glucoside precursors and further irreversible translocation into the reservoir keeps the glucoside concentration low inside the secretory cell.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the observed transport activity and localization of CpMRP.

claim: There is a first filter for specific glucosides at the hemolymph-exposed plasma membrane of the secretory cell, which might depend on a gradient-driven, energy-independent transporter.
source: By this fact, we suggest a first filter for specific glucosides (salicin, in the case of C. populi) at the hemolymph-exposed plasma membrane of the secretory cell, which might depend on a gradient-driven, energy-independent transporter.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation based on the observed selectivity and CpMRP's pacemaker function.

claim: CpMRP does not just dictate the transport rate of the transporter in the plasma membrane, rather, it determines the effectiveness and energy coupling of the entire sequestration process as a pacemaker.
source: Accordingly, CpMRP does not just dictate the transport rate of this transporter in the plasma membrane, rather, it determines the effectiveness and energy coupling of the entire sequestration process as a pacemaker.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on CpMRP's localization, transport activity, and the effects of its knockdown.

claim: The apical part of the secretory cell facing the lumen of the gland is a brush border membrane where storage vesicles are secreted via exocytosis.
source: Figure 6 further illustrates the fate of storage compartments. The apical part facing the lumen of the gland is a brush border membrane where storage vesicles are secreted via exocytosis (Noirot and Quennedy, 1974).
evidence: This is based on previous morphological studies cited and illustrated in the proposed model in Figure 6.

claim: The brush border membrane is invaginated and forms an extracellular room that is connected to the reservoir by the canal.
source: It is invaginated and forms an extracellular room that is connected to the reservoir by the canal.
evidence: This is based on morphological knowledge of the gland structure.

claim: CpMRP is present in the microvilli membrane.
source: That CpMRP is present in the microvilli membrane (Figure 3Bc), indicates that this is where the exocytosis of CpMRP-containing storage vesicles takes place.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical localization shown in Figure 3Bc.

claim: The exocytosis of CpMRP-containing storage vesicles takes place at the microvilli membrane.
source: That CpMRP is present in the microvilli membrane (Figure 3Bc), indicates that this is where the exocytosis of CpMRP-containing storage vesicles takes place.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of CpMRP in the microvilli membrane.

claim: After excreting the glucoside, CpMRP is most likely recycled to recover the protein in the dense packaging zone of storage vesicles/vacuoles.
source: After excreting the glucoside, CpMRP is most likely recycled to recover the protein in the dense packaging zone of storage vesicles/vacuoles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about protein recycling based on the observed distribution pattern.

claim: CpMRP is required to maintain defensive secretion in C. populi.
source: In the present study, we show that CpMRP is required to maintain defensive secretion in C. populi.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing loss of defensive secretions upon CpMRP knockdown.

claim: cpmrp-silenced larvae are defenseless because they lack defensive secretions.
source: Our results demonstrate that cpmrp-silenced larvae are defenseless because they lack defensive secretions.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing complete loss of defensive secretions.

claim: CpMRP is a transporter for plant derived glucoside precursors present in storage compartments as well as in the microvilli membrane of the secretory cell.
source: Functionally, CpMRP is a transporter for plant derived glucoside precursors present in storage compartments as well as in the microvilli membrane of the secretory cell.
evidence: This is supported by transport assays and immunohistochemical localization data.

claim: The identification of transporter sequences highly similar to CpMRP in the larval glands of other Chrysomelina species strongly implies that broad-spectrum ABC transporters involved in the sequestration of plant-derived metabolites are commonly present in the defense mechanism among Chrysomelina.
source: The identification of transporter sequences highly similar to CpMRP in the larval glands of other Chrysomelina species (P. cochleariae and C. lapponica) strongly implies that broad-spectrum ABC transporters involved in the sequestration of plant-derived metabolites are commonly present in the defense mechanism among Chrysomelina.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of highly conserved CpMRP homologs with similar expression patterns in related species.

claim: The sequestration of plant glucosides in Chrysomelina larvae is the result of the presence of several barriers with various degrees of selectivity.
source: These results, together with our published data, lead us to conclude that the sequestration of plant glucosides in Chrysomelina larvae is the result of the presence of several barriers with various degrees of selectivity: (1) those controlling the non-selective uptake of plant-derived glucosides from the gut lumen into the hemolymph and their excretion by the Malpighian tubules (together these barriers are relevant for nutrition), (2) those controlling the selective transfer from the hemolymph into the secretory cells and (3) those controlling the secretion into the reservoir where the broad-spectrum ABC transporter acts as a pacemaker.
evidence: This is a comprehensive model inferred from the current study's data and previous published work.

claim: The first barrier controls the non-selective uptake of plant-derived glucosides from the gut lumen into the hemolymph and their excretion by the Malpighian tubules.
source: These results, together with our published data, lead us to conclude that the sequestration of plant glucosides in Chrysomelina larvae is the result of the presence of several barriers with various degrees of selectivity: (1) those controlling the non-selective uptake of plant-derived glucosides from the gut lumen into the hemolymph and their excretion by the Malpighian tubules (together these barriers are relevant for nutrition), (2) those controlling the selective transfer from the hemolymph into the secretory cells and (3) those controlling the secretion into the reservoir where the broad-spectrum ABC transporter acts as a pacemaker.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and previous published work on glucoside transport.

claim: The second barrier controls the selective transfer from the hemolymph into the secretory cells.
source: These results, together with our published data, lead us to conclude that the sequestration of plant glucosides in Chrysomelina larvae is the result of the presence of several barriers with various degrees of selectivity: (1) those controlling the non-selective uptake of plant-derived glucosides from the gut lumen into the hemolymph and their excretion by the Malpighian tubules (together these barriers are relevant for nutrition), (2) those controlling the selective transfer from the hemolymph into the secretory cells and (3) those controlling the secretion into the reservoir where the broad-spectrum ABC transporter acts as a pacemaker.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed selectivity in sequestration and the proposed model.

claim: The third barrier controls the secretion into the reservoir where the broad-spectrum ABC transporter acts as a pacemaker.
source: These results, together with our published data, lead us to conclude that the sequestration of plant glucosides in Chrysomelina larvae is the result of the presence of several barriers with various degrees of selectivity: (1) those controlling the non-selective uptake of plant-derived glucosides from the gut lumen into the hemolymph and their excretion by the Malpighian tubules (together these barriers are relevant for nutrition), (2) those controlling the selective transfer from the hemolymph into the secretory cells and (3) those controlling the secretion into the reservoir where the broad-spectrum ABC transporter acts as a pacemaker.
evidence: This is supported by the functional characterization of CpMRP and its role in sequestration.

claim: This functional arrangement of a non-selective and a selective transporter in the defensive system seems to be common to many different leaf beetles.
source: This functional arrangement of a non-selective and a selective transporter in the defensive system seems to be common to many different leaf beetles (Discher et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: This peculiar import system facilitates the occasional host plant shifts of leaf beetles caused by parasite pressure.
source: This peculiar import system also facilitates the occasional host plant shifts of leaf beetles caused by parasite pressure (Agosta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary implications, supported by citation.

claim: After the shift to a new host plant only the selective transport element needs to adjust to the new metabolites; all other transport elements may remain unchanged due to their broad substrate tolerance.
source: After the shift to a new host plant only the selective transport element needs to adjust to the new metabolites; all other transport elements may remain unchanged due to their broad substrate tolerance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the evolutionary flexibility of the sequestration system.

claim: This assumption is supported by the observation of CpMRP homologs in different leaf beetles and beyond.
source: This assumption is supported by the observation of CpMRP homologs in different leaf beetles and beyond (Tribolium Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2008); however, none of them has been functionally characterized or localized as yet.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of CpMRP homologs and citation to genome sequencing data.

claim: None of the CpMRP homologs in different leaf beetles and beyond has been functionally characterized or localized as yet.
source: This assumption is supported by the observation of CpMRP homologs in different leaf beetles and beyond (Tribolium Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2008); however, none of them has been functionally characterized or localized as yet.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study relative to previous work.

claim: The identification of CpMRP as a non-selective pacemaker involved in the sequestration of plant-derived glucosides highlights how insects counter plant chemical defenses to evolve new functions for the plant-derived toxins as allomones.
source: The identification of CpMRP as a non-selective pacemaker involved in the sequestration of plant-derived glucosides highlights how insects counter plant chemical defenses to evolve new functions for the plant-derived toxins as allomones.
evidence: This is a broad interpretation of the evolutionary and ecological significance of the findings.
